description.narrative: In July 2020, the Jordanian government introduced amendments to Regulation No 90/2009 Of Domestic Workers, Cooks, Gardeners And Similar Categories which, among other reforms (1) clarifies the employer obligation to pay wages within 7 days of due date; (2) reform to working hours (the time during which domestic workers remain at the disposal of the employer is now calculated as part of "hours of work”); (3) improved privacy of domestic workers when filing a complaint; and (4) a clear right to terminate the contract in case of physical or sexual abuse or a violation of domestic workers’ fundamental rights. These legislative amendments are largely consistent with international labour standards, specifically the Domestic Workers’ Convention, 2011 (No. 189). The proposed legislation was made available for public consultation, including social partners, prior to the adoption of the new Regulations. With support from the Governments of UK and Switzerland, the ILO collaborated closely with the Ministry of Labour in 2018-19 to provide technical advice and advocacy on the importance of harmonizing national domestic worker legislation with the provisions of the Domestic Workers’ Convention, 2011 (No. 189). This technical support included presenting to an intra-Ministerial committee, formed to advise the Minister/Secretary General on legislative reforms, regarding Convention 189, as well as development of technical briefs and suggested legislative wording.

description.narrative:
The Al-Hassan Workers’ Centre (WC) is managed by the national Workers’ Centre Association, which includes government, employer, and union representatives, to provide services to garment workers in the Al-Hassan QIZ. During the biennium, the WC provided a number of new services, in particular relating to COVID-19 including: - Enabling over 600 migrant workers to complete online registration, book return tickets on evacuation flights and in completing self-declaration forms to facilitate airport entry. - Health emergency services to 35 migrant workers during the lockdown period, e.g., arranging ambulance services. - Registration to enable access to social security benefits: The WC supported more than 1,500 migrant workers in enrolling/correcting their information on the social security platform. This was particularly important since workers feared losing their benefits after leaving their jobs.
Improvements in existing services to protect labour rights of migrant workers were as follows: - Registrations on the official complaints platform -hemayeh - and referral of cases to the union, the labour office and Better Work Jordan. - Grievance documentation and follow-up: 150 individual and collective cases of grievances involving around 3,000 workers (around 900 were women workers) were received, processed and documented. These consisted of cases relating to: a) working conditions (delayed or non-payment of wages, deductions in wages, discrimination, refusal of sick leave provisions, denial of annual leave, verbal and sexual abuse, and failures to pay social security contributions, etc.); b) recruitment-related issues (collection of illicit recruitment fees and deceptive contracts), and illicit reprisals against workers who sought contract termination; and c) living conditions. With support from the UK government, during the period of 2020, the ILO provided support to the Al-Hassan Workers’ Centre to provide the new services in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as improved existing services, as highlighted in the results achieved column.
